645.title: Ardas close
645.hook: the history and hope of a whole people in one prayer
645.howItsDone: Sikhs say the full Ardas standing at the close of services and many daily prayers: it remembers the Gurus, the martyrs and the gurdwaras, makes the day's petition, and ends with good for all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, benti: inside the inherited prayer, the reason for today is yours to say. Today we close this part of the path and see the Ardas whole.

For thirty-five days we've taken one prayer apart, line by line, the way you might take apart a watch to see how it ticks. Now put it back together. Picture it all at once: a few minutes long, said standing, every day, in every gurdwara, in kitchens and hospital rooms and airports. And inside those few minutes, a whole people's story, from its first Guru to this morning's family asking for help with a new job.
screen: `THIRTY-FIVE DAYS, ONE PRAYER.` → `PUT IT BACK TOGETHER.` → `A WHOLE PEOPLE'S STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the Ardas as a map. It opens with lines from Guru Gobind Singh: first remember the Divine, then Guru Nanak, and it walks name by name through the ten Gurus, ending with the Guru Granth Sahib. Then it remembers. The Panj Piare, the five beloved ones. The four Sahibzade, Guru Gobind Singh's sons. The martyrs, named by what they endured, and those who served in the langar and kept faith under pressure. Then places: the five takhts, the seats of authority, and all the gurdwaras, including the ones left behind across the border. Then it asks: for the gift of Sikhi, faith, discernment, the Name; honor for the humble, strength for the weak, shelter for the shelterless. Then the petition, today's reason, in plain words. Forgiveness for any slip. And the last line: rising spirits, good for all. Look at the order: remember, then ask, then widen. A Sikh standing for the Ardas first places themselves inside a long line of Gurus, martyrs and ordinary servers. Only then do they bring their own small need, and they end by asking good for everyone. The history is the remembering; the hope is the last line. The words have grown over time. The Rehat Maryada gives the standard text, and the remembrance of martyrs reaches into the eighteenth century and beyond. That's part of the point: the Ardas is a living prayer that a people keeps adding its story to.
screen: `FIRST REMEMBER: THE TEN GURUS.` · `THE MARTYRS AND THE PLACES.` · `THEN ASK: FOR SIKHI, FOR TODAY.` · `END WIDE: GOOD FOR ALL.` · then, large: `A WHOLE PEOPLE PRAYS.`

segments.voice: Walk the map in your mind, one breath for each stop: the Gurus, the five beloved ones, the martyrs, the gurdwaras near and far, the humble and the weak, your own reason today, forgiveness for your slips, good for all. Go slowly, and let each stop be a picture, not a word. If you pray, you can close with a quiet Waheguru; if not, simply let the map rest in you.
Sahibzade, Guru Gobind Singh's sons: remembered in the Ardas alongside the Panj Piare and the martyrs, before it asks for the Name and for today, and ends with good for all.
Your line: a whole people prays. Tomorrow the path turns to hymns for every part of a life. Thirty-five days, one prayer, whole.

646.title: A shabad for every moment
646.hook: Sikhs mark birth, marriage and death with particular hymns
646.howItsDone: Sikhs sing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib in kirtan, and mark life's turning points with particular hymns: shabads of thanks at a birth, the lavan at a wedding, Kirtan Sohila at night and at a funeral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sahibzade, and the Ardas seen whole: remember, then ask, then widen. Today a new part of the path begins: hymns for a whole life.

Hum the first song you danced to at a wedding. Now the one playing in the car the summer you were seventeen. Now the one they played at your grandfather's funeral. Some songs get welded to moments like that: a private soundtrack. Sikh life has a shared one. The same hymns, sung at the same turning points, by family after family, generation after generation. A child born, a couple married, a life ended: each has its hymns, and some children can hum them before they can read.
screen: `THE SONG FROM THE WEDDING.` → `A PRIVATE SOUNDTRACK.` → `A SHARED ONE, FOR GENERATIONS.`

segments.voice: The word is shabad. It means word, and in Sikh usage it means two things at once. A shabad is a hymn, one composition from the Guru Granth Sahib. And the Shabad is the Word itself, the voice of the Guru, the presence of the One in sound. When a shabad is sung, Sikhs understand both are happening. These hymns are meant to be sung. The scripture is arranged by raag, musical mode, each with its own mood and, tradition says, its own time of day, and kirtan, singing the hymns with music, is at the heart of worship. Now look at a life. When a child is born, there are shabads of joy and thanks. When a couple marries, they walk four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib while the lavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung. At the end of every day, and at the end of a life, Kirtan Sohila is sung. Guru Nanak even wrote hymns for mourning, the alaahniaan, in Raag Vadhans on ang 578, which turn the old songs of lament toward the One. For the next five weeks, this part of the path walks through shabads like these: about wealth and greed, longing and friendship, night and morning, birth, marriage and death. Each is a hymn Sikhs reach for at a particular moment. The idea isn't to memorize a playlist. It's to have, for every moment, words and a melody that point beyond the moment itself.
screen: `SHABAD: A HYMN, AND THE WORD.` · `ARRANGED BY RAAG, TO BE SUNG.` · `BIRTH, MARRIAGE, NIGHT, DEATH.` · `FIVE WEEKS OF SHABADS FOR A LIFE.` · then, large: `A HYMN FOR EVERY MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Let one song tied to a memory play in your head, sacred or not, and notice where it takes you: a room, a face, a season. Kirtan works with that same pull of melody. If you know any shabad, even its first line or a single Waheguru sung to a tune, let it play next; if not, rest in the silence after your song.
Shabad. A hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Word itself. Sikhs sing particular shabads at birth, marriage, the close of each day and the end of a life.
Your line: a hymn for every moment. Five weeks of shabads start here. Six hundred forty-six days in.

647.title: Palaces of pearls
647.hook: if I had palaces of pearls and jewels, may I never forget You (Sri Rag M1, ang 14)
647.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, that without the Lord the soul burns and there is no other place, is often the line congregations repeat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shabad: a hymn, and the Word itself, sung at every turning of a life. Today, the first hymn of this stretch, and it begins in a dream house.

A real estate app, late at night. Infinity pool. Floor-to-ceiling windows over the ocean. A kitchen bigger than a whole apartment, a garden, room for everyone you love. Guru Nanak built a dream house too, in words. Near the start of the Guru Granth Sahib's main body, in Sri Rag, he raises a palace wall by jeweled wall. And then he asks one question about it.
screen: `A REAL ESTATE APP AT MIDNIGHT.` → `GURU NANAK BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE.` → `THEN ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The shabad is on ang 14. It begins, in effect: if I had a palace built of pearls, inlaid with jewels, its walls plastered with musk and saffron, sandalwood and aloe, a joy to come home to. Then the turn: let it not be that, seeing all this, I go astray, forget You, and Your Name no longer comes to mind. Then the refrain, the rahao, the line tradition treats as the hymn's center: without the Lord my soul burns to ashes; I asked my Guru, and I saw there is no other place. Then he does it again, three more times, each bigger. If the floor were paved with diamonds and rubies, and a beautiful companion waited on a jeweled bed. If I became a siddha, a yogi with miraculous powers, appearing and vanishing at will. If I became a sultan, raising armies, sitting on a throne, giving orders. Each time, the same ending: let me not forget You. Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say. He doesn't say palaces are evil, or beauty is a trap, or the rich are lost. Sikh teaching doesn't ask people to give up homes, families or work; the Gurus lived as householders. The danger he names is narrower and sharper: forgetting. A beautiful thing can fill the view so completely that the Giver drops out of the picture. The hymn doesn't ask for less. It asks to remember, even with more. And it's set in Sri Rag, a raag tradition associates with evening and seriousness: a grave melody for a dream house.

segments.voice: Build your dream house in your mind, the view, the kitchen, the morning light, whoever you'd want there, and enjoy it for a few breaths; you're allowed. Then ask Guru Nanak's question: in that house, would I still remember what matters most, still call my mother, still notice the person who cleans the pool? Let the house go gently, like setting down a heavy box, and if you pray, say Waheguru as you let go.
Rahao, the refrain, the line tradition treats as a hymn's center: here, after every luxury and power Guru Nanak imagines, it asks only this, that none of it make him forget the One.
Your line: may I not forget. Not less, just remembering. Day six hundred forty-seven, done.

648.title: Greed is a dog
648.hook: greed is a dog, falsehood a scavenger, cheating is eating carrion (Sri Rag M1, ang 15)
648.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its first-person confession, these are my deeds, is sung by the whole congregation about themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahao, the refrain at a hymn's center: may I not forget, even with more. Today Guru Nanak names what's doing the wanting, and gives it an unflattering face.

There's a dog in every neighborhood that knows exactly when the trash goes out. It was fed an hour ago and still stands at the gate, nose working, eyes on the bag. Not because it's hungry. Because it's a dog. Some of us have met a version of that dog inside: at a buffet, in a sale, scrolling past one more thing nobody needs. One page after the dream house, Guru Nanak names that dog out loud, and he doesn't soften it.
screen: `THE DOG AT THE GATE.` → `NOT HUNGRY, JUST A DOG.` → `GURU NANAK NAMES IT.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Sri Rag, on ang 15. Its first lines run, in effect: greed is a dog; falsehood is a scavenger; cheating is eating carrion. Slandering others is putting their filth in your own mouth. Anger is a fire that burns like an outcast's pyre. Then the punch: these tastes and this self-praise, these are my deeds, O Creator. The word for greed is lab, the hungry wanting that's never full. Two things to notice. First, the language is harsh on purpose. Guru Nanak takes the insults of his day, the names a caste society threw at people it looked down on, and throws them at the vices instead. It's the greed that's the dog, the lying that's unclean. The Gurus rejected caste outright, and here the shock of those words is turned around: the real lowness isn't in anyone's birth. It's in what a person does. Second, the surprise: the shabad is in the first person. Not you are greedy, not they are liars, but these are my deeds. The Guru speaks the confession himself, so anyone singing it says it about themselves, and nobody gets to point at the person across the hall. The refrain then turns to speech: speak in a way that brings honor; those whose deeds are good are called good at the Lord's door. So the dog isn't destiny. A dog can be noticed. It can be trained, or at least told no. The first step is just seeing it at the gate.
screen: `LAB: GREED, NEVER FULL.` · `INSULTS TURNED ON THE VICES.` · `THESE ARE MY DEEDS.` · `SPEAK IN A WAY THAT BRINGS HONOR.` · then, large: `MIND THE DOG.`

segments.voice: Think back over today or yesterday and find one moment when you wanted more than you needed: one more helping, one more purchase, one more scroll. Don't scold yourself; just see it, the way you'd see a dog at the gate, and notice where you felt it in your body. Breathe, and let it sit there without obeying it; if you pray, you can say Waheguru to it, quietly.
Lab, the hungry wanting that's never full: Guru Nanak names it, lying, cheating and slander, and confesses them as his own deeds, so everyone who sings it does the same.
Your line: mind the dog. Seen at the gate, it doesn't have to be fed. See you tomorrow.

649.title: The river and the fish
649.hook: You are the river, all-knowing; I am a fish, how can I find Your end (Sri Rag M1, ang 25)
649.tomorrow: The four watches of the night
649.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, wherever I look, there You are, is often repeated by the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lab: greed, the dog at the gate, confessed in the first person. Today, a gentler animal, and a tender picture from Guru Nanak.

Here's an old riddle: does a fish know it's wet? It has never been anywhere else. Water is above it, below it, inside its gills, carrying its food, holding up its weight. The one thing a fish can't do is step back and see the water. Guru Nanak, from the land of five rivers, wrote a hymn that swims close to that riddle. In it he doesn't play the river. He plays the fish.
screen: `DOES A FISH KNOW IT'S WET?` → `IT CAN'T STEP BACK AND SEE.` → `GURU NANAK PLAYS THE FISH.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Sri Rag, on ang 25. It begins, in effect: You are the river, all-wise, all-seeing; I am a little fish, how could I ever find Your end? The word for the fish is machhuli, a small fish, almost affectionate. Then the refrain: wherever I look, there You are; pulled out of You, I burst and die. That's the hymn in one picture. The fish can't measure the river or get outside it to see where it starts or ends. It doesn't need to. It just needs to stay in it. Out of the water, a fish doesn't become free. It suffocates. Then a very honest line. I don't know the fisherman, Guru Nanak says, and I don't know the net. But when pain comes, then I call on You. He admits what a lot of people would rather not: that we often remember the river only when we're flapping on the bank. And then a correction: You are present everywhere; I thought You were far away. Whatever I do is done in Your presence. Here's the gentle thing. Elsewhere Gurbani talks about separation from God as a kind of exile. This shabad suggests the separation is partly an illusion. The fish thinks the river is somewhere else because it's never seen it from outside, but it has never once been outside it. For Sikhs, that's what naam, remembering the Name, does: not bringing God close, but noticing how close God has been all along.

segments.voice: Watch water move: run a tap slowly, pour from one glass into another, or look at rain or a fountain, and if none is near, picture one clearly. See how it moves without effort and fills whatever shape it's given, then notice what surrounds you right now: air, light, the ground holding you up, all of it unasked for. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, a fish thanking the river.

Your line: a fish in the river. In the hymn, the river was never far. That's six hundred forty-nine.

650.title: The four watches of the night
650.hook: the four watches of the night as the stages of a life (Sri Rag M1, ang 74)
650.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Sri Rag pehre in kirtan, each stanza beginning with the watch of the night and addressing the listener as vanjaariaa mitraa, O merchant friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, machhuli, the little fish in the river: the One was never far. Today Guru Nanak lays a whole life over a single night.

Before clocks, a night was measured in watches. Guards on a city wall, sailors on a ship, merchants camped by the road: the dark was split into four stretches of about three hours, and each had someone awake. You'd know the watch by how the night felt. The first, still warm from the day. The deep middle ones. The last, cold and gray-blue, just before dawn. Guru Nanak took those four watches and turned them into a map of a human life.
screen: `A NIGHT IN FOUR WATCHES.` → `GUARDS, SAILORS, CARAVANS.` → `A MAP OF A HUMAN LIFE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is called a pehre, from pahar, a watch. It's in Sri Rag, beginning on ang 74, and Guru Nanak addresses it to vanjaariaa mitraa: O my merchant friend. The listener is a trader on a journey, sent out with capital, expected to come back with something to show for it. In the first watch, the hymn says, by the Lord's command you came into the womb, and there you remembered the One. You came into the world naked, and naked you'll go. In the second watch you forgot. You were passed from arm to arm, adored, as Krishna was in Yashoda's house, and your mother said: this is my son. In the third watch your mind was fixed on wealth and on your own young body, and the Name didn't come to mind. In the fourth watch the reaper comes. Nobody knows the hour, and the merchant's accounts are read: what did you trade your life for? It's a sobering hymn, and Sikhs sing it as one. But it isn't meant to frighten. Notice who is speaking: a friend, mitraa, calling out to a traveler while there's still night left. Naming the watches means a person can wake up in any of them. A child can remember. A busy parent in the third watch can stop. Someone very old, in the cold last stretch before dawn, can still turn. The question isn't how far the night has gone. It's whether you're awake for the watch you're in.

segments.voice: Sit with the four watches, beginnings, being carried and loved, building and earning, and the late cold watch for settling accounts, and ask honestly, without judging the answer: which watch am I in? Then ask the friend's question: what am I trading this watch for? If you pray, you can say Waheguru once and rest there.
Pahar, a watch, a quarter of the night: Guru Nanak's map of a life in four of them, womb, childhood, the busy middle, and the last watch, sung to a merchant friend while there's still time.
Your line: which watch am I in. Any watch is a good one to wake up in. Day six hundred fifty, done.

651.title: The four letters, whole
651.hook: Guru Arjan's longing letters to his father, read in full (Majh M5, ang 96–97)
651.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Majh shabad 'meraa man lochai gur darsan taaee' in kirtan, and tell the story of the letters from Lahore that led to his being named the fifth Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pahar: you can wake up in any watch of the night. Today the week closes with letters a son wrote while missing his father.

Early in the path we met young Arjan in Lahore. His father, Guru Ram Das, had sent him there for a family wedding and told him to stay until he was called. Weeks went by. No call came. Arjan wrote home in verse. Tradition says the first two letters never reached his father: his elder brother, Prithi Chand, kept them. So Arjan numbered the third. When Guru Ram Das read a letter marked three, he asked where one and two had gone. Today, all four stanzas, in order.
screen: `ARJAN, SENT TO LAHORE.` → `TWO LETTERS NEVER ARRIVE.` → `THE THIRD IS NUMBERED.`

segments.voice: They stand in Raag Majh, on angs 96 and 97, as one shabad of four stanzas. The first, in effect: my mind longs for a sight of the Guru. It cries like the chaatrik, the rainbird that tradition says drinks only falling rain; the thirst won't go, no peace comes, without seeing my beloved. Each stanza ends: I am a sacrifice, a sacrifice, to the sight of the Guru. The second: your face is beautiful, your words bring a deep, natural peace; it's been so long since this rainbird saw water. The third, the numbered one, is the sharpest. When I can't meet you for even a moment, it's the dark age for me. When will I meet you, beloved? The night won't pass; sleep won't come. The fourth was written after the reunion. Tradition says Guru Ram Das sent for him, and soon named him the fifth Guru. And the last stanza turns: by good fortune I've met the Guru, and found the eternal Lord within my own home. Read whole, the letters have a shape: longing, then memory, then near despair, then arrival. They can be heard as two loves at once, a son for his father and a soul for the One, and the shabad never pulls the two apart. Now, the week. The Ardas closed, a whole people's prayer. Then shabad, a hymn for every moment. Rahao: may I not forget. Lab. Machhuli. The four watches of a life. And the four letters: longing that gets an answer.
screen: `ONE: I CRY LIKE THE RAINBIRD.` · `TWO: SO LONG SINCE I SAW WATER.` · `THREE: A MOMENT AWAY IS A DARK AGE.` · `FOUR: FOUND IN MY OWN HOME.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE LONGING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you miss, someone far away, someone you've drifted from, someone who has died, and begin a letter to them in your head the way Arjan did, with the plain truth: I miss you. Add one thing you remember about them, then what the missing feels like, honestly. If you pray, you can hold them before the One with a quiet Waheguru.
Darshan, sight, seeing the beloved: Guru Arjan's four stanzas in Raag Majh long for it, like the rainbird, through the third letter's dark night, to the reunion, found in his own home.
Your line: the whole longing. Longing, memory, near despair, and then arrival. A week of hymns, complete.
